options: Running the same prompt once and trusting the first answer
Running the same chain-of-thought prompt multiple times independently and taking the majority answer
Rewriting the prompt until it produces exactly the same answer every time
Asking a different, unrelated question on each run
questions.explain: Self-consistency samples the same prompt several times and selects the answer that appears most often across those independent runs.

questions.q: In the lesson's train-distance example, why did the majority vote land on 195 miles instead of 185?
options: 195 was simply the first answer generated
The question was rewritten between runs
Two of the three independent runs agreed on 195; one run made an arithmetic slip and got 185
185 is not a valid number for a distance
questions.explain: Two out of three sampled runs converged on 195 miles; the outvoted run's arithmetic mistake was overridden by the majority.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does it mean when sampled runs disagree with each other?
options: It's meaningless noise that should always be ignored
It proves the model is broken and should not be used again
It's a signal that the question or prompt might need more work
It means the majority-vote technique has failed and cannot be used
questions.explain: Disagreement among sampled runs is treated as useful evidence that the task may need refinement, not just discarded as noise.

questions.q: How does the cost of self-consistency scale with the number of samples taken?
options: Cost stays flat no matter how many samples are taken
Cost scales directly with the sample count — 5 samples cost roughly 5 times as much as 1
Cost decreases as more samples are taken
Only the first sample incurs any cost; the rest are free
questions.explain: Each additional sample is a full additional model call, so cost and latency scale directly with how many samples are taken.

questions.q: When does this lesson recommend using self-consistency?
options: On every single prompt in an application, by default
Only for prompts under 50 words
Never — it was presented purely as a theoretical technique
For high-stakes answers where a wrong result is expensive, not as a default for every prompt
questions.explain: Because cost scales with sample count, the lesson recommends reserving self-consistency for cases where a wrong answer carries real cost.
